name: Aisha Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lead picker at a medical supplies warehouse on the edge of Harrow Vale, so think bandages, syringes, dialysis kits, all going out to clinics and hospitals. Since spring we've had six little robots that carry the totes between zones, and I'm the one who looks after them, which nobody else wanted. I start at six, check the robots' charge, sort out whatever they got stuck on overnight, then pick and train new starters. I love it, honestly, even if I'm paid the same as I was before the robots came.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you get on with the tech side?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day. When a robot throws an error code, I paste it into a chatbot and it usually tells me faster than the manual. I'm also doing an online course in mechatronics, which is mechanics plus electronics, in the evenings. The problem is money: I share a house with two friends, I've got about three weeks of bills saved, and the only other warehouse nearby pays even less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the robots we've got are the useful kind, and the rest was hype. At work I'd tell people our tote robots aren't going anywhere and neither are we. Online I'd post about how the gains from the robots we do have should show up in pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm stuck. I've been betting my evenings on the idea that robot skills would be worth something. If nothing changes, the course is still useful, but there's no rush of new jobs for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the mechatronics course anyway, because it's paid for and I'm two modules from the end. I'd ask my manager, Colin, for a pay grade that reflects looking after the robots. If he says no, I'd look at the hospital's own stores department, which pays a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit flat. I like change, and a world where nothing moves is kind of boring and still broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Colin, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've kept six robots running for eight months and saved him calling the supplier out maybe twenty times. That's worth a grade, or at least a skill payment. I'd have my list of call-outs printed, because he likes paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money pressure day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's the big one, then the car, which I need because there's no bus at six. I send my mum 40 a month when I can. One bad month and I'm on the overdraft, which has happened twice this year.

say: Our tote robots are the **useful kind**, and the rest was hype.
The gains from the robots we have should **show up in pay**.
think: My **evening course** was a bet that robot skills would pay off.
If nothing changes, I'm still **broke** with no new jobs to move into.
do: Finish the last **two modules** of the mechatronics course.
Ask Colin for a **robot-care pay grade**, with a printed list of call-outs.
Look at the **hospital stores** department if Colin says no.
feel: **Uneasy and flat**; a world where nothing moves is boring and still broke.
S0.quote: A world where nothing moves is kind of boring and still broke.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** has outrun her pay: she does extra work for no extra money.
The **overdraft** twice this year keeps money pressure live even in the quiet picture.
She argues for **shared gains** but acts individually, with printed evidence.

steps.text: Finish the last two modules of the mechatronics course
Ask Colin for a pay grade for looking after the robots
Apply to the hospital stores department if the grade is refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get trained, and to get the company to pay for it. At work I'd be the one showing people the new screens. Online I'd push for public training money, because most pickers can't afford evening courses like I can barely afford mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me if I play it right. The planning and ordering jobs shrink first, and the robots spread slowly, which is exactly when a warehouse needs someone who understands both. The danger is the company hiring a technician from outside instead of paying me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course and then ask the robot supplier about their field technician training, since they're always short. I'd use AI tools to write up our robot faults properly, so the data shows what I've been doing. And I'd join the union, because I want the training fund in writing, not just for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a bit nervous. It feels like the door I've been leaning on finally opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push for training money for everyone. Why not just look after yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my mate Jade on the packing bench is smarter than me and has a kid, so she can't do evenings. If only people like me get through, that's not fair, it's just lucky. I'd be in the union meetings for people like Jade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the supplier wanted you to travel a lot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it. I've got no kids, the house share is month to month, and travelling around fixing robots sounds more fun than picking syringes. The worry is the car and the money for the first few months before the pay kicks in.

say: This is the moment to **get trained**, and the company should pay.
Most pickers can't afford evening courses, so we need **public training money**.
think: Slow robots and fast office change are **good for me** if I play it right.
The danger is the company hiring an **outside technician** instead of paying me.
do: Ask the robot supplier about **field technician** training after the course.
Log robot faults with **AI tools** so the data shows her work.
Join the **union** to get a training fund in writing.
feel: **Mostly excited**, a little nervous, like a door finally opening.
S1.quote: My mate Jade on the packing bench is smarter than me and has a kid, so she can't do evenings.
fieldNote: She sees **Steady Disruption** as her opening, while her thin savings still make her careful.
Uses AI to make her **hidden work visible** through fault logs.
Her progressive views show up as concern for **colleagues** who lack her time.

steps.text: Ask the robot supplier about field technician training
Log every robot fault with an AI tool for proof of work
Join the union and push for a written training fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a plan from government, now, like a public jobs guarantee, because nobody else has one. At work I'd tell people to learn the robots, since that's the last job standing. Online I'd be arguing that companies and the public should share ownership of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd have five good years, maybe. In 2028 the AI could probably diagnose the robots better than me, so my chatbot trick becomes the robot's own job. By 2031 the robots fix each other, or near enough, and I'm 32 with a forklift licence and a certificate nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in now: finish the course, get the supplier job, and save every penny of the higher pay. I'd look at moving to the city where the robot firms are, because Harrow Vale has nothing. And I'd join anyone campaigning for a share of the profits going to workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be moving, not frozen. Fast is scary when you've only got three weeks in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said thinking AI might diagnose the robots better than you by 2028. What's left for you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands bit, until 2031: unjamming a wheel, swapping a battery, crawling under a rack. That's three years of being the person the AI sends to do the physical stuff. It's not glamorous, but it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving to the city with three weeks saved. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd only go with a job offer and a room lined up, maybe sleeping on my cousin Nadia's sofa for a month. I'd sell my car, since the city has trains. Scary, but I've moved with less.

say: Government needs a **jobs guarantee** now, because nobody else has a plan.
Workers and the public should **share ownership** of the robots.
think: By **2028** AI may diagnose robots better than me.
By **2031** I'm 32 with a certificate nobody needs.
do: Get the **supplier technician job** and save all the extra pay.
Move to the **city** with a job offer, selling the car.
Join campaigns for a **profit share** for workers.
feel: **Anxious** but moving, not frozen, with only three weeks saved.
S2.quote: I'd have three years of being the person the AI sends to do the physical stuff.
fieldNote: She clearly sees her **three-year window**: AI takes the thinking part, hands last until 2031.
Willing to **move** with little money, which few in her position would risk.
Her politics lean towards **shared ownership**, not only regulation.

steps.text: Take the robot supplier's technician job and save the extra pay
Move to the city with a job offer and sell the car
Campaign for workers to get a share of robot profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, if you start now. At work I'd tell the younger pickers to do the course I did. Online I'd keep pushing for public training funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me. I'd get maybe eight years out of robot maintenance before the robots really don't need people. That's a whole career stage, and I could save enough to choose what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, take the supplier job within a year, and put 150 a month aside. I'd start teaching the robot basics to others at the warehouse, maybe as a paid trainer. And I'd use AI to plan my next move after 2034, probably something with people rather than machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before a big trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Something with people rather than machines. Like what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe teaching at the college, or health work, since I already know the clinic side from the supplies. I'd ask an AI to map out what's left in 2034 and then talk to real people doing it. I trust the AI for options, not for decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your thin savings change in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd better. With supplier pay and no car payments I could get to three months saved in two years. That's the first time in my life I'd have that.

say: **Five years** is enough to get ready if you start now.
Younger pickers should do the **course** I did, and the state should fund it.
think: Robot maintenance gives me about **eight years** of work.
That's long enough to **save** and choose what comes next.
do: Take the **supplier job** within a year and save 150 a month.
Offer to train others as a **paid robot trainer**.
Use AI to map out jobs **after 2034**.
feel: **Uneasy in a good way**, like before a big trip.
S3.quote: I trust the AI for options, not for decisions.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **career stage** and real savings for the first time.
Plans a second move into **people work** before the robots arrive.
Uses AI as a **map**, not a decision-maker.

steps.text: Take the robot supplier job within a year
Save 150 a month towards three months of bills
Offer paid robot-basics training to pickers at the warehouse
Ask an AI to list jobs likely left after 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and most people will waste it. At work I'd tell people to start something now, anything. Online I'd push for the government to plan the decade, not just react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years I could do robot work and still have time for a second training. By 2039 I'd be 40, which is fine for a new start. My worry is other people, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supplier job, save, and in five or six years start a nursing or paramedic course, since the clinic side interests me. I'd keep using AI daily for study. I'd stay in the union to keep training money flowing for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your worry is other people. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pickers like Jade, and the older guys on the loading bay who've been there 20 years. They won't go to college at 50. Ten years doesn't help someone who can't use the ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm fine and she doesn't need to worry, which would be mostly true. She'd still worry. She'd want me to have a 'proper' job, and a nurse would count.

say: **Ten years** is a gift, and most people will waste it.
The government should **plan the decade** instead of just reacting.
think: I could do **robot work** and still fit in a second training.
My worry is for **other people**, not myself.
do: Work the **supplier job** and save for five or six years.
Start a **nursing or paramedic** course after that.
Stay in the **union** to keep training money flowing.
feel: **Uneasy but mostly hopeful**; she'd sleep fine.
S4.quote: Ten years doesn't help someone who can't use the ten years.
fieldNote: She plans **two careers** across the decade, robots then care.
Her unease is about **older colleagues** who can't retrain at 50.
Her mother's idea of a **proper job** quietly steers her towards nursing.

steps.text: Save from the supplier job for five or six years
Start a nursing or paramedic course around 2032
Push the union to keep training money open to all

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to move fast with three weeks of savings, and moving fast costs money. What would help is a public training fund and a bit of money to live on while you retrain, so it's not just people with savings who make it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who gets paid for looking after the robots. Right now it's nobody. I've kept six robots running for eight months on a picker's wage.

headlineQuote: I've kept six robots running for eight months on a picker's wage.
portrait: Aisha, 27, is a **lead picker** who looks after six tote robots at a medical supplies warehouse.
She uses **AI daily** and studies mechatronics in the evenings, but has three weeks saved.
She sees robot maintenance as her **window**, and is willing to move to the city.
She stays mostly uneasy and turns **anxious** only in the 2028 picture.
Her politics show in **concern for colleagues** who can't retrain like her.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because moving fast costs money she doesn't have.
whatWouldHelp: A **public training fund** with living money while people retrain.
